stances.claim: The Constitution prohibits not deprivation per se but deprivation without due process -- a critical distinction often lost in public discourse that conflates due-process protections with absolute protection against deprivation, when in fact lawful deprivation (e.g., post-trial conviction) is constitutionally permissible.
stances.rhetorical_move: definitional-clarification at front (precise scope of due-process clause)

stances.claim: The 1987 Constitution's iron-clad suspect protections -- strict warrant requirements, strict-construction exceptions, Miranda rights, exclusionary rule for illegally obtained evidence -- were motivated by fresh memory of martial law abuses and aimed at protecting the innocent, especially the poor and marginalized.

The libertarian pendulum has swung too far -- producing police timidity (out of administrative/criminal liability fears) that has enabled a rise in criminality, with grafters/killers/rapists/drug lords misusing the Constitution's liberality, exacerbated by prosecutorial/judicial failure (ignorance, apathy, laziness, corruption), missing witnesses, and lawyers who thrive in technicalities rather than justice.

The consequent public revulsion conflates due process with overdue process (costly suits, tiring delays, technicalities, long-winded trials, interminable appeals, unwelcome acquittals, plain injustice), driving people to extralegal/extrajudicial shortcuts -- the solution requires police, prosecutors, lawyers, and judges to cooperate, think outside the box, moderate the pendulum, and craft innovative ways to provide quality and speedy justice without the 'over' in due process.
stances.rhetorical_move: diagnostic-then-prescriptive arc (revulsion explained + multi-actor coordination prescribed)

notable_anecdotes: The column's central title-and-thesis pun 'Overdue process' -- the most concise statement of the analytical frame in any CJ column on this theme, condensing the entire diagnosis into a single word-play coinage.

The libertarian-pendulum metaphor: 'the libertarian pendulum swung too much to the opposite direction, resulting in the timidity of the police' -- the column's central diagnostic image, attributing post-martial-law overcorrection.

The multi-actor failure catalog: 'even when police officers strictly observe constitutional rights, some prosecutors and judges, out of sheer ignorance, apathy, laziness, or corruption, fail the justice system. So, too, witnesses are bribed, lose their memory, or otherwise disappear. Many lawyers thrive in technicalities and delays' -- distributing blame across the entire criminal-justice ecosystem.

The list of overdue-process discontents: 'costly suits, tiring delays, inexplicable technicalities, long-winded trials, interminable appeals, unwelcome acquittals and plain injustice' -- using accumulated grievances to physicalize public frustration.

The 'extralegal and extrajudicial shortcuts' phrase -- an unambiguous implicit reference to the Duterte-era extrajudicial killings without naming them, preserving editorial discretion while still flagging the phenomenon.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban examines the Bill of Rights' due-process and search-and-seizure protections -- and how the post-1987 libertarian pendulum has swung too far. He clarifies that the Constitution prohibits not deprivation per se but deprivation 'without due process'; arrest and search warrants require judges to personally determine probable cause under oath with specified place and items, with strict-construction exceptions only for in flagrante delicto and hot pursuit (per his Oct 6 column), Miranda rights to silence and counsel, and exclusion of evidence obtained through torture, force, violence, threat, or intimidation. These iron-clad protections were motivated by fresh memory of martial law abuses, aimed at protecting innocent suspects especially the poor and marginalized. But 'the libertarian pendulum swung too much to the opposite direction,' producing police timidity from admin/criminal liability fears, and 'the net result is the rise in criminality. Grafters, killers, rapists and drug lords misuse the liberality of the Constitution to evade liability.' Even when police strictly observe rights, prosecutorial and judicial failure (ignorance, apathy, laziness, corruption), bribed or missing witnesses, and 'many lawyers thrive in technicalities and delays, rather than in their sworn duty to do justice to everyone' compound the breakdown. The consequence is general revulsion against democratic methods -- overlooking that 'means are as important as ends' -- with due process equated with 'costly suits, tiring delays, inexplicable technicalities, long-winded trials, interminable appeals, unwelcome acquittals and plain injustice'; in frustration, people turn to 'extralegal and extrajudicial shortcuts' (an unmistakable if unnamed reference to the Duterte-era killings). To solve the revulsion to 'overdue process,' police, prosecutors, lawyers, and judges must cooperate, think outside the box, moderate the pendulum swing, and craft innovative ways to provide quality and speedy justice for all -- safeguarding precious constitutional rights without the 'over' in due process.
